articles.title: UFC fighting cage rises on White House lawn for US and Trump celebrations
articles.summary: The UFC bout at the White House marks the 250th anniversary of the US and President Donald Trump’s 80th birthday.
articles.body:
Yet another White House construction project is under way in the United States, though this one is meant to be only temporary.

Crews are erecting an octagon-shaped cage on the South Lawn that will host next month’s Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) bout, marking the nation’s 250th anniversary and President Donald Trump’s 80th birthday .

list 1 of 4 Messi’s GOAT statue in India to be removed over safety concerns

list 2 of 4 Messi set for more tests ahead of World Cup but Argentina are optimistic

list 3 of 4 World Cup broadcast hopes boosted in India as Zee Entertainment in talks

list 4 of 4 Scotland fans book 20 school buses for games at ‘inaccessible’ US World Cup

Online renderings depict what the completed, wire-mesh-fence-ringed fight space is expected to look like before the June 14 event. It will be ringed by a red, white and blue stage under a towering arch featuring stars-and-stripes patterns and two large screens showing the action live.

The cage and stage will themselves be surrounded by thousands of temporary seats, including ringside space for a full marching band that can set the entire scene to blaring music.

The project is part of a series of events celebrating the semiquincentennial of the Declaration of Independence’s signing on July 4, 1776. Other planned functions include an IndyCar race that will pass by the White House and the Great American State Fair taking place on the National Mall.

Trump has said the finished UFC project will feature “a 5,000-seat arena right outside the front door of the White House”.

Additional large screens broadcasting the fights will be set up in a park at the nearby Ellipse, and the UFC has said it plans to issue as many as 85,000 free tickets to accommodate spectators at both locations.

“I have never seen anybody want anything so much as people want those tickets,” Trump said recently of demand to attend the UFC fight, adding, “That’s gonna be something.”

The card has been panned by fans online as underwhelming, featuring just two championship fights. Brazil’s Alex Pereira will meet France’s Ciryl Gane for the interim UFC heavyweight title. Then, Spanish-Georgian lightweight champion Ilia Topuria takes on interim champ Justin Gaethje, one of just two Americans who currently hold even a share of the UFC’s 11 championship belts.

The octagon and surrounding structures are the latest project in the White House building boom Trump is leading.

The president’s other efforts to leave his mark include tearing up part of the Rose Garden to make room for a patio space reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, affixing partisan plaques to the wall of the colonnade for a Presidential Walk of Fame, redoing the toilet attached to the Lincoln Bedroom and renovating the Palm Room, placing new flagpoles on the north and south lawns and demolishing the entire East Wing for a sprawling ballroom.

The president also wants to repaint the Eisenhower Executive Office Building beside the White House and build a 250-foot (76-metre) arch at the nearby Lincoln Memorial – the same monument where weigh-ins for the upcoming UFC fight are scheduled to take place, bout organisers say.

articles.title: Luke Littler: Wayne Mardle hails Premier League champion for opening up about struggles, says he has 'no weaknesses'
articles.summary: Luke Littler questioned future after tough times in Brighton and Manchester during Premier League season; world No 1 beat Luke Humphries 11-10 in gripping final to lift trophy for second time in three years; Wayne Mardle says Littler playing at "peak level" and can win in different ways
articles.body:
Sky Sports Darts pundit Wayne Mardle hailed Luke Littler's honesty and talent after his thrilling 11-10 victory over Luke Humphries in the Premier League final.

Littler secured the title for the second time in three years and then became emotional in his on-stage interview as he discussed under-performing in Brighton earlier in the season, a week after being involved in an argument with Gian van Veen in Manchester.

The 19-year-old was knocked out in the quarter-finals on both of those nights and revealed after his triumph in London that he was considering his future at that point after booing from the crowd.

  • Premier League Darts: Full 2026 results
  • Darts in 2026: Key dates and results
  • Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app
  • Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW

Littler said: "I was sat at home saying to [girlfriend] Faith, 'I don't want to do it any more, just the crowd every week'. I said to her, 'I'm down bad'."

Speaking following Littler's win over Humphries in the 17th week of competition, Mardle said the champion's admission of his struggles was a "step forward".

'I have nothing but admiration for this teenager'

Mardle told Sky Sports: "There is more that goes on in a Premier League than just turning up week after week. It is a rollercoaster for every player, whether you are winning games or struggling.

articles.title: England netball star Helen Housby ruled out of this summer's Commonwealth Games in Glasgow with back injury
articles.summary: England will be without Helen Housby for the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow; experienced goal shooter suffered a back injury in April; watch the Netball Super League live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
England star Helen Housby will miss the Commonwealth Games due to injury.

The Games are set to take place in Glasgow from July 23 until August 2, but England will be without their mainstay goal shooter.

In April it was revealed that Housby would miss an "extended period" of the Suncorp Super Netball season in Australia due to a back injury, with further scans confirming she will be unable to compete this summer.

  • Results and fixtures for 2026 season
  • Netball Super League standings
  • Sky Sports' Off the Court Podcast

Housby, who famously scored England's last-minute winner when they won gold at the 2018 Commonwealth Games, says she is "devastated" to miss out in the Glasgow event.

"Representing Team England is an honour and holds some of my proudest and fondest memories," she said.

"Despite the setback I'm more determined than ever to come back stronger and get back on court as soon as possible, especially with the World Cup in Sydney on the horizon.

"I'm lucky to be surrounded by an incredible support system and I'm very grateful for the love I've received from those closest to me, England Netball, the New South Wales Swifts and the Vitality Roses fans back home.

"I'm excited to see what our girls can achieve this summer and will be giving everything I can off the court to support them in Glasgow. I truly believe our squad can beat anybody and I'm looking forward to watching as a fan this time around."

articles.title: Ferrari sign Leclerc on new long-term contract before home F1 Monaco GP
articles.summary: Charles Leclerc has extended his contract with Ferrari for an undisclosed length, having joined the F1 team in 2019.
articles.body:
Charles Leclerc will continue to race for Ferrari after ⁠the Italian Formula One team announced a long-term contract extension before his home Monaco Grand Prix.

The 28-year-old Monegasque has driven for the Maranello-based outfit in F1 since ⁠2019, winning eight races, and his last contract extension came in 2024.

list 1 of 4 World Cup contenders: Are Morocco ready to go all the way this time?

list 2 of 4 Cape Verde football team arrives in the US for the World Cup

list 3 of 4 US artist sues FIFA over destruction of Dallas whale mural for World Cup

list 4 of 4 ‘We aren’t the big favourites,’ Brazil’s Casemiro says

“I couldn’t be happier to continue this journey with Scuderia Ferrari HP. It has always been so much more than just a team to me,” Leclerc said in a statement issued by Ferrari on Wednesday.

Leclerc is currently third in the 2026 drivers’ championship but 56 points behind Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli, who is 43 ahead of teammate and closest rival George Russell after winning the last four races.

He has raced more times for Ferrari (155) than any other driver in the team’s history, other than now-retired seven-time world champion Michael Schumacher, and also ranks ‌second for pole positions behind the German.

Ferrari did not specify the duration of his new contract, saying only that Leclerc would continue for the “coming seasons” in the championship.

“Charles has been part of the Ferrari family for many years now and this renewal feels like something very natural for us,” team principal Fred Vasseur said.

“Over these seasons, we have seen him grow to become not only one of the strongest drivers in Formula One, but also a person who is completely at one with ⁠the team and everything Ferrari represents.

“We know how much this project means to ⁠him and we are happy to continue working towards our shared goals.”

Leclerc joined the Ferrari Academy in 2016, won the Formula Two title in 2017 and made his F1 debut with Ferrari-powered Sauber (now Audi) in 2018.

Leclerc’s teammate is the UK’s seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton, who ⁠joined from Mercedes last year on a multi-year contract and is expected to continue next season, when he will be 41 years old.

Hamilton is fourth in the ⁠standings, three points behind Leclerc.

Ferrari have not taken a Grand Prix ⁠victory since 2024, or a championship since 2008, but Hamilton won a Saturday sprint race in China last season and finished second in Canada last month.

Leclerc has had two podium finishes this season – third in Australia and Japan – and will be heavily fancied for his ‌home race this weekend, with Ferrari expected to be competitive at the slowest circuit on the calendar, where top speed is less of a factor and grid position is crucial.

Growing up in the principality, Leclerc in 2024 ‌became ‌the first local to win the Monaco Grand Prix in the championship era and has taken pole there three times in the last five years.

articles.title: Netball Super League Grand Final: Manchester Thunder's Karen Greig looks to cement legacy with win over London Pulse
articles.summary: Karen Greig is looking to add to Manchester's plethora of silverware when her Thunder side take on the London Pulse at the Co-op Live Arena in Manchester; Watch the Pulse vs Thunder Grand Final live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
The AO Manchester Thunder face the London Pulse in the Netball Super League Grand Final - and a title win on home soil is in touching distance for Karen Greig and her side.

Since her appointment as Thunder director and CEO in 2016, she has made three Grand Finals and won two titles - including an unbeaten league campaign in 2022 - but a title win in front of a home crowd at the Co-op Live Arena could be her crowning achievement.

They face a familiar foe in the Pulse. The Thunder have beaten Sam Bird's side on two out of three occasions this season, most recently beating them 60-56 in the major semi-final just under two weeks ago - setting up a tantalising title decider between undoubtedly the league's two best teams.

A win for Greig, then, begs the question - would a third title in her 10-year tenure make her Manchester's most successful coach?

  • Netball Super League standings
  • Results and fixtures for 2026 season
  • Sky Sports' Off the Court Podcast

"Pep [Guardiola] probably was [the most successful], wasn't he? He left after 10 years," Greig told Sky Sports. "But Manchester clubs this season have had a really, really successful year.

"[Manchester] City didn't quite get over the line in the league, but they won a couple of trophies - the FA Cup - and the women also won in the league and the cup.

"So I'm like, come on, guys, we've got to get amongst that silverware - and hopefully we can.

"I don't think I'd be the most successful coach in Manchester, but hopefully we'll add more to the legacy that our city brings."

Greig, though, knows the challenge that a reinvigorated Pulse side will pose, with her opponents having beaten the Loughborough Lightning 60-56 in the Preliminary final.

"That's the best I've seen Pulse play for a long time this season [against the Lightning]. There have been sticky points for them, and I really think they bought their A-game on Saturday.

"I thought they were, they were brilliant in attack and in defence.

"I do think it's going to be a game of chess.

"I've just got to be smart with how we're operating, how we're taking their lines, to not giving them the opportunities to run at things.

"We'll throw a couple of tweaks in there, but nothing outrageous, as you know, we want the players to be comfortable with how we're operating."

Bird: I'm backing us

After the Pulse's latest loss against the Thunder, head coach Bird gave a damning verdict on a "terrible" performance from her side - but her harsh words seem to have acted as a launchpad for their subsequent two wins to book their place in the Grand Final.

"I had so many messages of thank you for being authentic - but all I'm ever bothered about is really about how we represent the club and getting the most out of our athletes in the club.

"The leaders [in the dressing room] that you would expect to stand up said 'we know that wasn't good enough'. I think it's really important when it comes from the players.

"The fact that they knew that they could perform better was just really encouraging to me.

"I just knew then that we would be putting our right foot forward for the Loughborough game, and so it proved."

The reigning champion Pulse have been there and done it. Even after two straight losses to the Thunder - and a hostile Manchester crowd in the final - Bird is confident in her team's ability to get over the line.

"We want to make sure we're able to play the game we can play, and when we're on form - I'm backing us.

"If we can be nice and tidy and really respond well to the umpiring, not let the occasion overwhelm how we want to play, then I think it should be a cracking game."

articles.title: Tamsin Greenway: Manchester Thunder's Sophie Fawns 'a joy to watch' - huge pressure on Australians who come to play in Super League
articles.summary: Australian Sophie Fawns joins Tamsin Greenway on latest episode of Sky Sports' Off The Court podcast, following her player of match display in Super League Grand Final as Manchester Thunder beat London Pulse; Former England head coach Tracey Neville also provides glowing assessment
articles.body:
Manchester Thunder's Sophie Fawns has been an "absolute joy to watch," says Tamsin Greenway, as she welcomed the Grand Final player of the match onto the latest episode of the Sky Sports Off The Court podcast.

Thunder beat London Pulse 54-51 in a thrilling Grand Final to win the Netball Super League title on Saturday.

The match was poised at 51-51 with less than a minute remaining, but Australian Fawns stepped up to sink a dramatic winner and guide Thunder to a record-equalling fifth NSL title.

"She's [Fawns] been an absolute joy to watch," Greenway said.

"Just the impact she had in that final. Sophie Fawns is the game-changer here and we'd spoken about it a lot beforehand as well.

  • Results and fixtures for 2026 season
  • Netball Super League standings
  • Sky Sports' Off the Court Podcast

"She came on in the Grand Final, halfway through that second quarter, and had 18 points in total.

"She scored eight out of 10 in the one-point zone, but more importantly, five out of eight in the super-shot with that massive two-pointer at the end of the game.

"Two minutes to go, level pegging after Karen Greig's timeout. I mean, Fawns spoke about the pressure there was playing in Australia, and she spoke about loving the game over here, but you know that was still a massive moment in front of all of those people.

"The impact and technical change early from Karen Grieg was brilliant, because they knew what they could get from Sophie Fawns."

Former England international and head coach Tracey Neville was also full of praise for Fawns on Off the Court.

"She's the one that's always brought on to make the difference and what an absolute top girl," Neville said.

"As soon as Sophie Fawns came on, I felt the crowd and the team lifted.

"The size of her, the impact that she had, the possession, but even that role on centre pass as well, and then when they brought Lois Pearson on to complement her with the speed, I just felt it opened up so much.

"I think in that second quarter they got caught a lot just running down into pockets and they played a lot of a possession game. The change in speed or tempo was so effective.

"Sophie Fawns, every time she gets the ball in hand, do you ever think she's going to miss? I felt like a centre just walking back to the circle whenever she got the ball in the circle."

Fawns: Big expectations and pressure on Australians coming to Super League

Speaking to Greenway on Off the Court, Fawns touched on the difficulty for Australian players coming into Super League, and the way she has managed such expectation and succeeded.

"I'd spoken to a few of the Aussie girls who have been here already and they kind of said it's that expectation that no one talks about but everyone also talks about," Fawns said.

"That you've come from Australia, so everyone expects you to be absolutely phenomenal.

"That was one of the first conversations I had with Karen Greig [head coach]. She was like: 'I think you're an amazing player, but I don't expect anything of you.'

"She also said: 'there is no pressure at the end of the day, because realistically in terms of netball minutes, you're still quite young. We can't expect you to put out, in the first round, 60 minutes of amazing netball, and that's okay. We're here to build with you.

"I think just to have those conversations, it eased the pressure that I felt.

"She literally was like, just go and have fun, like, don't deep it, it's netball."

'Moving to play in England is one of best decisions I ever made'

Fawns added in a wide-ranging discussion with Greenway that her decision to travel to Manchester and ply her career here is one which has proven inspired.

"I really think that coming over to England was one of the best decisions I've ever made, and I'm so grateful that I did it.

"For me, coming from playing in SSN (Suncorp Super Netball - professional league in Australia) and being a pressure-moment shooter or playing those 20 minutes, I had a different kind of role.

"I wanted to progress my game into being more of a full-time player, and I know I was always brought out to run around, bring a bit of chaos, bring that kind of speed.

"I remember my first few training sessions, Karen was a bit like: 'Whoa, you can slow down, it's okay, we don't have to run at everything.'

"I had to remember it was about lasting 60 minutes, not just five at a time.

"So for me, it was just about learning that craft and learning how to be a little bit smarter of a player, and I really think Karen was one of the best coaches to learn from for that."

"For me, coming from playing in SSN (Suncorp Super Netball - professional league in Australia) and being a pressure-moment shooter or playing those 20 minutes, I had a different kind of role.

"I wanted to progress my game into being more of a full-time player, and I know I was always brought out to run around, bring a bit of chaos, bring that kind of speed.

"I remember my first few training sessions, Karen was a bit like: 'Whoa, you can slow down, it's okay, we don't have to run at everything.'

"I had to remember it was about lasting 60 minutes, not just five at a time.

"So for me, it was just about learning that craft and learning how to be a little bit smarter of a player, and I really think Karen was one of the best coaches to learn from for that."

articles.title: Luke Littler: World Matchplay defending champion believes he can dominate like Phil Taylor ahead of semi-final
articles.summary: Luke Littler stormed into the semi-finals of the World Matchplay with a thumping win over Josh Rock and has set his sights on dominating the sport in the same fashion as Phil Taylor; you can watch the World Matchplay live on Sky Sports in Blackpool until July 26
articles.body:
Luke Littler says he will dominate darts in the same way Phil Taylor did if he continues his sparkling form.

A scintillating Littler progressed to the semi-finals of the World Matchplay on Thursday with a dominant 16-7 win over Josh Rock, averaging 109.57 with a 53 per cent success rate on the doubles.

On Saturday 'The Nuke', who scored 17 180s against Rock in Blackpool, will face Dirk van Duijvenbode in the semi-final - live on Sky Sports.

The world No 1 is aiming to become the first player since Michael van Gerwen in 2016 to go back-to-back in Blackpool, with few betting against him.

Following his win, Littler was asked by Sky Sports if he is confident he can dominate the sport in the same fashion as all-time great Phil Taylor did.

  • World Matchplay Day Six: As it happened!
  • Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results 📅
  • Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app 📱
  • Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺

Littler said: "Yeah, I feel like I can. My averages of 113 and 109 come with the big finishes and the scoring power is there as well with the 180s. As long as I can keep it up, I'm sure I will dominate."

He was then asked about the prospect of being the first player in history to approach £3m on order of merit.

Littler replied: "I checked the rankings the other day. I think if I beat Dirk [van Duijvenbode], then I will go into that £3m mark.

"As long as I'm playing like this and producing numbers, it's going to take something special from another player to beat me. I've just got to keep going."

Littler currently holds the World Darts Championship, UK Open, Premier League and Masters titles.

He is also defending the Matchplay, Grand Slam, Grand Prix and the Players Championship Finals.

Such is his form there are suggestions he could be set for the greatest ever Matchplay.

On talk of the prospect, he said: "I wouldn't say I'm aware of it. I saw something yesterday that Gezzy [Gerwyn Price] is up in the ranks for most legs played.

"In this competition you don't want to be at the top, you want to be down at the bottom. You don't want to win by two clear legs, you just want to get the job done. As long as I perform like that, I'll be happy."

Immediately after Thursday's win, he said: "I feel really good up on the stage, preparations beforehand are going really well, just relaxing, playing, relaxing again. I'm just glad I can perform on the biggest stages."

articles.title: World Matchplay darts: Gerwyn Price issues title warning to 'ruthless' Luke Littler after reaching Blackpool semi-finals
articles.summary: Luke Littler remains pre-tournament favourite to defend his title at the World Matchplay; Gerwyn Price faces Gian van Veen in Saturday's semi-finals as he looks to reach his first Blackpool final since 2022; watch throughout the weekend live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Gerwyn Price insists he can thwart Luke Littler's bid for back-to-back World Matchplay titles and believes some players ‘make it too easy’ for the defending champion.

Price booked his first World Matchplay semi-final since 2022 with a 16-12 win over Ross Smith at the Winter Gardens, where the 'Ice Man' fired a 102.78 average and closed out victory with a four-leg burst.

The Welshman faces world No 3 Gian van Veen in the last four, with the winner of that semi-final progressing to face either Littler or Dutchman Dirk van Duijvenbode in Sunday's best-of-35 leg final.

  • Latest World Matchplay Darts results, schedule 📅
  • Gerwyn Price books semi-final spot - as it happened
  • Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app 📱
  • Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺

Littler defeated Price in every Premier League fixture between them this season and a final-set decider in the World Masters semi-finals, while 'The Nuke' remains unbeaten in PDC major matches over 20 legs since his 2024 World Championship final loss.

The world No 1 remains overwhelming favourite to become the first player since Michael van Gerwen to defend his World Matchplay crown, having posted a 109.57 average in his win over Josh Rock, although Price insists he can be stopped.

"I think there's a lot of players that can get to that [Littler's] level," Price told reporters after his quarter-final win.

"Is there anyone who can do it as long as him? I think I can and I think there's a couple of players, but he's ruthless at the minute - these 109, 110 averages just look so easy for him.

"I think some players play into his hand and just let him play with his rhythm. It's horses for courses, and sometimes you have to play your game, you have to play the game and you have to play the moments.

"Sometimes, people make it a little bit too easy for him."

More to come in Van Veen showdown?

Price built a commanding 12-8 lead over Smith in a quarter-final where he threatened to pull further ahead, then found himself level at 12-12 until finishing strongly to reach the last four.

"I was delighted with the way I played the majority of the game, but there's a couple of legs that I let slip and could have come back to haunt me in the end," Price added.

"I'm thinking I should be 13-7 or 14-6 or whatever it is, because I did waste opportunities and probably shouldn't think like that. I'm just happy to get a win, but frustrated a little bit."

Van Veen admitted he needs to improve after his quarter-final victory over 16-13 James Wade, where he posted a 93 average and also blew a four-leg advantage before closing out victory.

"It felt very poor!" Van Veen admitted to Sky Sports. "My scoring was so terrible. I was so lucky James wasn't scoring as well and my finishing got me through. A win is a win.

"The 118 finish - I really needed it. It was a tight battle but I'm glad I got the job done. Hopefully tomorrow I will be a lot better."

What's next?

The 2026 Betfred World Matchplay continues at the iconic Winter Gardens on Saturday, with the two semi-finals being played over the best-of-33 to decide who progresses through to Sunday's best-of-35 final.

Defending champion Littler continues his bid for back-to-back titles when he faces Van Duijvenbode, through to the last four at this event for the first time, with Price playing Van Veen in the opening semi-final.

Who will win this year's World Matchplay Darts? Watch throughout the weekend live on Sky Sports. Live coverage continues Saturday from 7.30pm on Sky Sports Action and around 9pm on Sky Sports Main Event. Stream darts and more top sport with NOW.

articles.title: Commonwealth Games:  England cruise past Northern Ireland to open netball campaign as Scotland fall to New Zealand
articles.summary: England limber up for Sunday’s big Commonwealth Games netball clash against Australia by sweeping aside Northern Ireland in their opening group game; Eleanor Cardwell scored 35 goals and vice-captain Liv Tchine added 25
articles.body:
England thrashed Northern Ireland 83-34 on the opening day of the Netball pool stage at the Commonwealth Games but Scotland were beaten by New Zealand.

England ran out comfortable winners at The Hydro, with all 12 players taking to the court in a confidence-building performance.

Head coach Anna Stembridge saw her side take a 24-7 lead at the first quarter break, which soon became 41-18 at half- time.

  • Results and fixtures for 2026 season
  • Netball Super League standings
  • Sky Sports' Off the Court Podcast

Jayda Pechova and captain Fran Williams both impressed, while Lois Pearson, Sasha Glasgow and Liv Tchine linked up nicely.

Half-time substitute Eleanor Cardwell top-scored with 35 goals from 37 shots, with the squad now focusing on the ultimate test against defending champions Australia on Sunday.

"Getting that first win and performance under our belts was important," said Stembridge. "We'll make sure we close the loop in our debrief and then turn our full focus to Australia tomorrow."

"Australia are world No 1 for a reason, and we have a huge amount of respect for them," she continued.

"We feel well prepared and will be ready to respond to whatever tactics they bring. It's exciting to think about the matchups and the challenges we can pose as well.

"Ultimately, you want to play against the best and coach against the best.

"Those are the opportunities that test you and help you improve."

Vice-captain Tchine added: "It was great to see everyone putting into practice what we've been working on in training. Everyone came out and gave everything.

"I think we needed that. We played together well and got those first-game nerves out of the way. Everyone knows what it's like in that opening match, so now we're ready to focus on Australia tomorrow."

Meanwhile, Scotland suffered a 74-44 defeat to New Zealand in their Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games opener, though the remaining group matches against lower-ranked opposition offer a chance to bounce back.

articles.title: Luke Littler hails World Matchplay defence as one of the 'best weeks of his life' after historic Gerwyn Price victory
articles.summary: Luke Littler became the first player in a decade to defend his title at the World Matchplay; he broke the record for the most 180s hit in the tournament and set the highest-ever average recorded in a final with 111.53
articles.body:
Luke Littler has hailed his historic run at the World Matchplay as "one of the best weeks of his life" after a record-breaking 18-9 over Gerwyn Price in Blackpool.

It capped off a week in which Littler has broken record after record. The 19-year-old started his week with a 109 average against Niko Springer and then took things to new heights with a 113 average and nine-darter against Nathan Aspinall.

A 109 average against Josh Rock followed, before he demolished Dirk van Duijvenbode in the semi-finals.

  • Latest World Matchplay Darts results, schedule 📅
  • Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app 📱
  • Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺

Littler then became the first player in a decade to retain the title at the Winter Gardens, defeating Price while rewriting the record books in the process.

Littler fired an 111.53 average which smashed the tournament scoring record, previously set by Phil Taylor in 2010, leaving Littler continuing his run of winning every PDC TV major in 2026.

He also posted six ton-plus finishes and broke his own tournament record for most 180s, hitting 66 across the week.

Not only that, he broke the £3m earning barrier during his run to the final, with the latest win enhancing his hopes of sweeping every ranked major in a calendar year.

They are numbers to simply behold and Littler himself counts them as some of the best he has ever posted in his life.

"It has been a crazy week - it has been one of the best weeks of my life," Littler told Sky Sports.

"The darts I have played - it has not been easy. It has been tough. The stats may look like it is easy but when you are on this stage, it is hot, it is not easy.

"I have played some of the best darts of my life.

"Two years ago, I had that first round defeat to Michael which was not the best result, The last two years, I have come here with the family and we have done it again.

"It is definitely, I feel like it is the best version of myself. I have just been playing so well.

Littler: I am heading to the Pro Tours!

Littler said on the opening night of the World Matchplay that, if he defended his title, he would then have to head to the Pro Tour in order to attempt the clean sweep which would include having to defend his Players Championship Finals win in Minehead.

With that in mind, the world No 1's next stop is Leicester, rather than the planned trip to Spain.

"I don't think my dad is too happy because we were meant to be going to Spain but now we will be going to Leicester for some Pro Tours," he added.

"Coming into the tournament I had won every major so far so this is what I wanted to do.

"I have been checking the Pro Tour rankings. I know there is four in Leicester I have got to go to now.

"If I don't qualify I will get grilled, if I qualify I will get grilled anyway so who knows what is going to happen."

What's next?

The next PDC ranked TV major is the BoyleSports World Grand Prix from September 28-October 4 at the Mattioli Arena, Leicester, live on Sky Sports. Littler returns as defending champion after last year's victory over Luke Humphries in the double in, double out event.

The Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton (November 14-22) and the World Darts Championship (December 10-January 3) are also both live on Sky Sports, with Littler looking to retain his titles in both events. Stream darts and more top sport with no contract.

articles.title: World Matchplay Darts: Luke Littler thrashes Gerwyn Price 18-9 to defend title with record-breaking display in Blackpool
articles.summary: Luke Littler becomes the first player since Michael van Gerwen to win back-to-back World Matchplay titles; Littler broke Phil Taylor's record for the best tournament average during an 18-9 win over Gerwyn Price at the Winter Gardens in Blackpool
articles.body:
Luke Littler capped off a remarkable title defence at the World Matchplay Darts with an impressive 18-9 victory over Gerwyn Price in Blackpool.

Littler fired an 111.53 average and nailed 12 maximums in a dominant display against the 2022 runner-up, posting six ton-plus finishes in a high-scoring final to become just the fourth player in history to win back-to-back World Matchplay titles.

The winning margin looked set to be larger when Littler raced into an 11-3 lead, with Price - who averaged 104.97 in his performance of the tournament - delivering a battling display but falling to his second runner-up finish in four years.

  • World Matchplay Darts final recap: As it happened!
  • Latest World Matchplay Darts results, schedule 📅
  • Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app 📱
  • Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺

The 19-year-old averaged 109 or better in all five matches during his perfect week at the Winter Gardens and smashed the tournament scoring record, previously set by Phil Taylor in 2010, leaving Littler continuing his run of winning every PDC TV major in 2026.

Littler broke his own tournament record for most 180s and extended his lead at the top of the PDC rankings by reclaiming the Phil Taylor Trophy and £225,000 first prize, having broken the £3m barrier during his run to the final, with the latest win enhancing his hopes of sweeping every ranked major in a calendar year.

How Littler closed out historic title

Price said ahead of the final that he felt like he could beat Littler with his A-game, although the 'Ice Man' couldn't come close to his opponent during a historic final.

The first three legs went with throw before Littler followed a sensational 167 checkout - his first bullseye finish of this year's tournament - by taking out 110 to hold throw in the next, opening a 4-1 lead despite Price averaging over 109 in the mini session.

Littler added back-to-back 11 darters and responded to Price holding throw in the next by taking out tops-tops for a third ton-plus finish in the first nine legs, then pulled further ahead in an extraordinary scoring burst.

The world No 1 posted 128 and 127 finishes and took just 47 darts to breeze through a dominant four-leg streak, lifting him 11-3 ahead, although Price dug in by winning successive legs to try and spark a comeback.

Price stayed within six legs of Littler before the 19-year-old produced another devastating late surge, firing in a stunning 148 checkout before breaking throw in the following leg. Littler then sealed a historic victory in style, pinning an 81 finish on the bullseye.

Victory is Littler's 10th consecutive win over Price and 28th consecutive win at PDC major matches over 20 legs, a run stretching back to the 2024 World Championship final, with the world No 1's record-breaking display sending an ominous warning to his rivals heading into the rest of the season.

Price praises 'one in a million' Littler

Littler, speaking to Sky Sports: "It has been a crazy week - it has been one of the best weeks of my life. The darts I have played - it has not been easy. The stats may look like it is easy but when you are on this stage, it is hot, it is not easy.

"I have played some of the best darts of my life. I feel like it is the best version of myself - I have just been playing so well!

Price, speaking to Sky Sports: "Luke [Littler] is one in a million. I think I played pretty decent. In that game I missed a couple of opportunities but the bull checkouts, the 167, was a big turning point even though it was early in the game.

"If anyone wants to boo this kid there is something wrong with them. He is fantastic for this sport. I wish he wasn't as good as he was, because I would have won a couple more tournaments.

"I probably could have pinched a few more legs but his finishing was just effortless. I hope there is nobody else like him coming through, because he is ridiculous! It was a great week for me but I am a little bit gutted!"

What's next?

The next PDC ranked TV major is the BoyleSports World Grand Prix from September 28-October 4 at the Mattioli Arena, Leicester, live on Sky Sports. Littler returns as defending champion after last year's victory over Luke Humphries in the double in, double out event.

The Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton (November 14-22) and the World Darts Championship (December 10-January 3) are also both live on Sky Sports, with Littler looking to retain his titles in both events. Stream darts and more top sport with no contract.

Luke Littler capped off a remarkable title defence at the World Matchplay Darts with an impressive 18-9 victory over Gerwyn Price in Blackpool.

Littler fired an 111.53 average and nailed 12 maximums in a dominant display against the 2022 runner-up, posting six ton-plus finishes in a high-scoring final to become just the fourth player in history to win back-to-back World Matchplay titles.

The winning margin looked set to be larger when Littler raced into an 11-3 lead, with Price - who averaged 104.97 in his performance of the tournament - delivering a battling display but falling to his second runner-up finish in four years.

  • World Matchplay Darts final recap: As it happened!
  • Latest World Matchplay Darts results, schedule 📅
  • Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app 📱
  • Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺

The 19-year-old averaged 109 or better in all five matches during his perfect week at the Winter Gardens and smashed the tournament scoring record, previously set by Phil Taylor in 2010, leaving Littler continuing his run of winning every PDC TV major in 2026.

Littler broke his own tournament record for most 180s and extended his lead at the top of the PDC rankings by reclaiming the Phil Taylor Trophy and £225,000 first prize, having broken the £3m barrier during his run to the final, with the latest win enhancing his hopes of sweeping every ranked major in a calendar year.

How Littler closed out historic title

Price said ahead of the final that he felt like he could beat Littler with his A-game, although the 'Ice Man' couldn't come close to his opponent during a historic final.

The first three legs went with throw before Littler followed a sensational 167 checkout - his first bullseye finish of this year's tournament - by taking out 110 to hold throw in the next, opening a 4-1 lead despite Price averaging over 109 in the mini session.

Littler added back-to-back 11 darters and responded to Price holding throw in the next by taking out tops-tops for a third ton-plus finish in the first nine legs, then pulled further ahead in an extraordinary scoring burst.

The world No 1 posted 128 and 127 finishes and took just 47 darts to breeze through a dominant four-leg streak, lifting him 11-3 ahead, although Price dug in by winning successive legs to try and spark a comeback.

Price stayed within six legs of Littler before the 19-year-old produced another devastating late surge, firing in a stunning 148 checkout before breaking throw in the following leg. Littler then sealed a historic victory in style, pinning an 81 finish on the bullseye.

Victory is Littler's 10th consecutive win over Price and 28th consecutive win at PDC major matches over 20 legs, a run stretching back to the 2024 World Championship final, with the world No 1's record-breaking display sending an ominous warning to his rivals heading into the rest of the season.

Price praises 'one in a million' Littler

Littler, speaking to Sky Sports: "It has been a crazy week - it has been one of the best weeks of my life. The darts I have played - it has not been easy. The stats may look like it is easy but when you are on this stage, it is hot, it is not easy.

"I have played some of the best darts of my life. I feel like it is the best version of myself - I have just been playing so well!

Price, speaking to Sky Sports: "Luke [Littler] is one in a million. I think I played pretty decent. In that game I missed a couple of opportunities but the bull checkouts, the 167, was a big turning point even though it was early in the game.

"If anyone wants to boo this kid there is something wrong with them. He is fantastic for this sport. I wish he wasn't as good as he was, because I would have won a couple more tournaments.

"I probably could have pinched a few more legs but his finishing was just effortless. I hope there is nobody else like him coming through, because he is ridiculous! It was a great week for me but I am a little bit gutted!"

What's next?

The next PDC ranked TV major is the BoyleSports World Grand Prix from September 28-October 4 at the Mattioli Arena, Leicester, live on Sky Sports. Littler returns as defending champion after last year's victory over Luke Humphries in the double in, double out event.

The Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton (November 14-22) and the World Darts Championship (December 10-January 3) are also both live on Sky Sports, with Littler looking to retain his titles in both events. Stream darts and more top sport with no contract.

articles.body:
Final results from the 2026 Betfred World Matchplay, held at the Winter Gardens in Blackpool.

Defending champion Luke Littler became the first player since Michael van Gerwen to retain the title in Blackpool, producing a tournament-record average as he sealed an emphatic 18-9 victory over Gerwyn Price.

Littler previously came past Niko Springer in his tournament opener ahead of beating Nathan Aspinall in a second-round thriller, before thrashing Josh Rock and Dirk van Duijvenbode to breeze through to the final.

  • Luke Littler goes back-to-back in Blackpool!
  • Recap: Litter v Price - as it happened!
  • Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app
  • Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW

2022 runner-up Price edged past Martin Schindler in his tournament opener and then improved to beat Rob Cross in the next round, before defeating Ross Smith to continue his record of reaching every TV major semi-final this season.

Price saw off Gian van Veen 16-13 to reach his first major TV final since 2023, with the victory lifting him to world No 4 and seeing him leapfrog Jonny Clayton as the highest-ranked Welshman.

The event featured the top 16 players from the PDC Werner Rankings Ladder as well as the best 16 players from the one-year ProTour rankings.

Prize purses for the 2026 event have been boosted to £1m, with the winner set to pocket £225,000. Littler reaching the final guarantees him becoming the first player in history to break £3m in prize money.

articles.title: Luke Littler: What does rest of 2026 look like for world No 1 as he targets the clean sweep of majors after World Matchplay triumph
articles.summary: Luke Littler is targeting a clean sweep of majors in 2026 but what exactly does he need to still win? He has already won the World Darts Championship, UK Open, Premier League, Masters and the Matchplay in 2026
articles.body:
When Luke Littler arrived in Blackpool for the World Matchplay he made one thing clear: the outcome of this tournament would determine how the rest of his 2026 unfolded.

"The next nine days will decide if I go to the Players Championship Finals," Littler told Sky Sports on opening night.

"If I don't win this then I'm not going back to Minehead for the Players Championship Finals. If I do win this then I will have to go to some Pro Tours and try and get in there."

articles.title: Luke Littler: Target Darts explain the science behind World No 1's phenomenal success
articles.summary: "He's back-to-back world champion, what he could do in the sport is entirely up to him" - James Tattersall, CEO of Target Darts, says the world is Luke Littler's oyster; you can watch the BoyleSports World Grand Prix live on Sky Sports from Sept 28 to Oct 4 in Leicester
articles.body:
Want to know the secret behind the success of darting phenom Luke Littler?

Littler has spearheaded darts' surge towards the mainstream since he broke on the scene with his debut run to the 2024 World Championship final as a 16-year-old.

Darts manufacturer Target Darts has supported the global superstar since the age of 12. In February 2024, the teenager signed a multi-year mega-deal reported to be worth up to £20 million - the most lucrative the sport has ever seen.

  • Luke Littler dominates Gerwyn Price to close out historic World Matchplay defence
  • Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results 📅
  • Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app 📱
  • Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺

Littler possesses a generational talent when it comes to playing darts and Sky Sports pundit Wayne Mardle has said "he's probably the most natural naturally gifted player I've ever seen in my life".

Since the moment the Warrington-born star first held a dart, he's become a record-breaker and history-maker.

James Tattersall, CEO of Target Darts, says both the company and Littler are "aligned" in where they want to see the future of darts go.

Speaking at an event in which Target have set out a vision to inspire 100 million people to play darts by the end of the decade, he explained the process of how Littler sat down with chairman Garry Plummer, the design team, and engineers to build darts to perfect his game.

"I think some of the inspiration was drawn from Adrian Lewis' darts and the pixel grip, which is a unique grip that Target has and that worked its way into building up Luke's original G1," said Tattersall. "That was the barrel, but over the years Luke's tweaked it and challenged us to improve it. The point length has changed, the shaft and flight have changed to a K-Flex system before his first World Championships."

F-Flex is a one-piece flight and shaft innovation that screws into the back of the barrel.

Tattersall explained: "What it helps you do is when you're throwing darts together in such tight groupings like Luke does, the thing you want to avoid is that dart coming in and deflecting off the dart that's already in the board and the K-Flex helps reduce those deflections substantially.

"And longer points - it's like the balance of the dart and how it flies and how it lands through the air. I think another part of it is it keeps the barrel section of the dart further away from the treble and that creates more space in the board."

Talent vs Equipment?

"His talent is all down to him," says Tattersall. "I think when you're talking about the equipment, we're talking about making Luke comfortable with all of that talent and giving him the right equipment that he's confident with to use and just to get those last few percentages, but Luke's an extraordinary player regardless."

With two world titles in three visits to Alexandra Palace, and 14 major titles to his name, Littler is well on his way to joining Phil Taylor as a legend of the sport.

The problem for his rivals is that he is still getting better after the Warrington star crushed Gerwyn Price 18-9 to retain his Betfred World Matchplay title in Blackpool on Sunday.

Littler was in imperious form as he set a new record for the final with an average of 111.53, lifting his average for the tournament as a whole to 111.04 to break Phil Taylor's previous high mark of 106.31.

The win keeps Littler on course for a clean sweep of trophies in 2026 having already won the World Championship, UK Open, Premier League and the Masters.

The supporting cast behind Littler

Littler's management have invested in sports psychologists, nutritionists, performance coaches, and biomechanics in order to get the most out of their talent, and the teenager has benefitted in every area to help support his game.

"Mentality is absolutely key. We want to protect the players. The stage is lonely up there, and darts is a gruelling sport," Tattersall said.

"It's a bit like a penalty shootout, but every single time you're throwing a dart. It's such a closed skill, and it's so repetitive. Your mindset's got to be really, really clear, and you get those big momentum swings, you think you're about to checkout the double, you miss by a millimetre, your opponent throws in a big 170 checkout, and that's a punch in the stomach. It's how do you recover from that for the next leg? That's sports psychology, and it's crucial in all sports. I don't know why it's a surprise that it should not be in darts."

'We want to learn about action - not create robots'

With biomechanics, the cameras observe how a player throws darts, with sports science data helping ways of working on the technique in order to improve.

Target have ideas but Tattersall insists implementing them will not turn the Luke Littlers of this world into robots.

"That's the last thing we want to do," he said. "What we want to do is discover and learn about the sport, and learn about that action, because why is it that there are different throwing techniques?

"If you look at something like golf, where you know suddenly you come along with the Vardon grip [or overlapping grip], and that becomes almost the only way to hold a golf club.

"I think the high jump has got that really famous example of how the sport, science, innovated, [Fosbury flop], you ended up with that kind of one technique point.

"I think there will always be different ways of throwing a dart, and there will be different ways of improving those different styles, and maybe that particular style is because you're tall, and maybe that particular style is because you've got longer arms, we don't know yet, but that's what we're going to find out, and then use that data accordingly."

Zoe Burton, Chief Transformation Officer at Target Darts, says Littler is already inspiring the next generation with his natural talent, although the company are slowly moving towards a performance technology system, which is currently being tested on a number of players.

"If you look at a young person and you think of their journey as they get into a sport, you need an inspiring player - that person who they look up to - and can almost aspire to be. Luke Littler provides that," said Buton.

"You need a natural talent, but that gets you so far. Then it's determination and I think psychology as well.

"What makes a star player become a great and world-class player is actually their ability to focus under pressure and make those doubles It's never going to be robotic."

articles.title: Commonwealth Games: Adam Ramsay-Peaty's emotional reaction to bronze medals shows event still matters, says Laura Kenny
articles.summary: Dame Laura Kenny admits Adam Ramsay-Peaty should have acknowledged his competitors after bronze medal wins, but six-time Olympic medallist says emotional interviews show importance of Commonwealth Games
articles.body:
Adam Ramsay-Peaty's emotional reaction to his Commonwealth Games performances has illustrated just how important the event is to athletes, according to Dame Laura Kenny.

Three-time Olympic swimming champion Ramsay-Peaty was visibly tearful after picking up two bronze medals at this summer's downsized tournament, first in the 100m breaststroke and then again in the 50m.

After previously going eight years unbeaten in the 100m, Ramsay-Peaty was clearly disappointed with his performance, admitting "nothing makes sense" in interviews afterwards.

  • Commonwealth Games Glasgow 2026 LIVE
  • Download the Sky Sports app 📱
  • Not got Sky? Get Sky Sports or stream with no contract on NOW📺

The 31-year-old's takes have received a mixed reception from fans watching on - but now-retired six-time medal-winning Olympic cyclist Kenny believes Ramsay-Peaty showed "strength" to show up under "a lot of pressure."

"He was emotional after the first one and obviously to bring yourself back round, to come back up and perform the way he did for a bronze medal, that takes strength in itself," Kenny told Sky Sports News.

"The emotion that he showed in those interviews post-bronze just shows how much the Commonwealth Games means to these athletes.

"You're performing under the pressure, you're coming back from ultimately being a superhero and held to such a high standard that people almost expect you to win gold every single time.

"Coming from someone who has experienced that, the pressure of that can be a lot. You're under the spotlight for two weeks every two years and that is a lot of pressure to have to deal with.

"Throw into the mix stuff that has or hasn't happened in his personal life, I think it is a lot for you then to come out and perform."

Ramsay-Peaty has recently vowed to let his swimming do the talking following his high-profile wedding to Holly Ramsay, daughter of chef Gordon Ramsay, and a subsequent family fallout.

He also drew criticism for a failure to congratulate his fellow athletes in his interviews after his bronze finishes.

Kenny understands the negative reaction to Ramsay-Peaty's comments at the Glasgow Games.

"I probably would have started with saying well done to the athletes that got gold and silver," she said.

"But I can totally understand because, in the heat of the moment, when you are getting asked questions immediately after you've performed, it's so emotional, anything comes out."

These Games were originally scheduled to take place in Victoria, Australia, but the organisers pulled out due to spiralling costs, with Glasgow stepping in to pick up hosting duties.

After going ahead with just 10 sports, there have been fears for the future of the event, but Kenny believes it remains important.

"Athletes want to compete," Kenny, who retired in 2024, said. "For me, taking away the Commonwealth Games would have been one last chance to compete. It would have been one less multi-sport event that we had on the calendar.

"The Commonwealth Games is one of the only times para-athletes and able-bodied athletes coincide, so why would we take that away? It's also got the added element that the home nations are split up, so actually it's really nice to compete for Team England.

"You've got all these National Lottery funded athletes that ultimately want to train and race and compete, so why would we want that off the calendar?"

articles.summary: After Luke Littler's dominant World Matchplay victory, Laura Turner and Chris Murphy debate on the Love The Darts podcast whether 'The Nuke' is the most dominant sportsperson in the world right now
articles.body:
Teenage dart sensation Luke Littler has left the darts world questioning if anyone will ever get near him again after winning the World Matchplay Darts on Sunday.

'The Nuke' stormed to victory in Blackpool, winning the competition for the second year in a row and seeing off final opponent Gerwyn Price 18-9.

Littler being in total control at a darts competition is nothing new. He's won every PDC major title in 2026 so far, and his World Matchplay performance has made it very difficult to argue he's not head and shoulders above his competitors.

His mind-blowing performances have sparked debate over where he ranks in the sporting world, leading Sky Sports' Love The Darts podcast pundits, former darts player Laura Turner and darts commentator Chris Murphy, to debate whether he is indeed the most dominant sportsperson in the world right now.

"It's a very difficult question, how do you measure dominance?" Murphy said. "Darts seems to have more majors than any other sport, if you're doing it on major titles, but then again if you just took the top four and made it fair, he wins what you might call the Grand Slam titles.

"He holds them all and he's on course to have a clean sweep of every title so of course he does. I think yes [he is the most dominant]."

Murphy then named two other sporting stars that come close to giving Littler a run for his money - tennis world No 1 Jannik Sinner and his golf equivalent, Scottie Scheffler - but concluded neither can touch him.

"Looking at other sports, we've mentioned tennis, Sinner maybe he's in the conversation," he said. "Scheffler in golf has been No 1 for a long time, but I don't think any of them get near Littler."

Turner agreed, pointing out how rare it is to have two English people dominating a sport in both the men's and women's editions at the same time.

"It's very hard to say no [he isn't the most dominant] isn't it," Turner said. "From a women's darts point of view actually I think [Women's World Matchplay winner] Beau Greaves is unbelievably dominant, she's just picked up the Matchplay in Blackpool. She won 17 out of the 24 titles available in that qualification process as well.

"She's been on a run of 114 consecutive wins, it took Fallon [Sherrock] at a 102 average just to stop that run. Beau is very dominant.

"In darts at the moment I personally think we're very lucky, I know Beau is on the Pro Tour as well. I can't think of another sport where at this moment in time, anyone that is dominating in the way they are."

While Turner and Murphy have been wowed by Littler this month, they believe the teenager still has a while to go until he can call himself darts' greatest ever.

Asked if he is the best darts player to ever do it, Murphy replied: "No, and this is where I think we need to zoom out a little bit. Potential to best the greatest? Possibly, but I don't think it's especially close yet to be honest.

"It's not criticism of his abilities and talents, it's just simple arithmetic I suppose. Phil Taylor's title tally, 16 world titles, spanning across four different generations of darts players, and he's had to reinvent himself for different games in different eras."

Taylor, who retired in 2018, holds the record for the most darts world titles. Littler, meanwhile, has two, winning the PDC World Darts Championship in 2025 and 2026 after bursting on the scene in 2024.

Laura agreed that Littler has a way to go yet to edge Taylor, adding: "All of us suffer from recency bias. There's a lot of people don't forget that never engaged in darts to the level they are before Luke Littler came onto the scene.

"Ultimately, Phil has played through different generations, I don't want to say mind games but you know you can get under people's skin a bit more.

"Ability wise, and all the accolades he has won over all those years, you have to say Phil is the greatest ever darts player we've had.

"Luke Littler perhaps one of the most dominant sports people at this time."

articles.title: Luke Littler insists 'clean sweep very much on' as he attends Warrington mural unveiling days after World Matchplay win
articles.summary: Luke Littler attends unveiling of mural he "didn't want to see" in Warrington just four days on from storming to World Matchplay victory; 'The Nuke' has his sights set on unprecedented clean sweep amid stunning form
articles.body:
Luke Littler believes "not many" can stop him in the form he showed at the World Matchplay as he sets his sights on a 2026 majors clean sweep.

The 2026 PDC World Championship winner was frightenedly good in Blackpool, beating darts legend Phil Taylor's Matchplay record average of 106.31 with 111.04.

"I'm feeling very good," Littler told Sky Sports at the unveiling of his mural in Warrington on Thursday. "With performances like that, not many can stop me. Obviously, a tournament average of 111 was really, really good."

  • Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results 📅
  • Download the Sky Sports app 📱
  • Not got Sky? Get Sky Sports or stream with no contract on NOW📺
  • Is Littler the most dominant sportsperson in the world?

The 19-year-old has won every PDC title in 2026 so far - the World Championship, World Masters, UK Open, Premier League, World Cup and now the World Matchplay.

As it stands, he could still achieve an unprecedented clean sweep of eight ranking titles in the calendar - and Littler admitted that record is on his mind going forward, starting with working on qualifying to defend his Players Championship Finals title.

"The clean sweep is very much on," he said. "I think you can only look at what's coming up. For myself now, I can't go and say 'I'm going to win the World Championships'. That's in another five or six months.

"You've just got to look at what's in front of you. I've got a nice two-week holiday to Orlando tomorrow as well to look forward to. I think the clean sweep, it's very much on.

"As long as I qualify for Minehead, whether I win the World Series, the European, it's all coming up. It's a busy end of the year, but we'll see."

If a clean sweep was achieved, where does Littler think it would rank in terms of sporting achievement?

"For darts, I think it would be up there with probably one of the best," he said. "No one's ever done it. That's what I'm going for. I like to break all these records."

Littler's mural was unveiled in his hometown Warrington just four days on from breezing past Gerwyn Price to win yet another title in Blackpool.

The teen darts sensation signed his name on the artwork, took time to pose with fans for photos and played darts in front of the crowd present.

However he is still keeping himself grounded, both mentally and physically.

"[The mural is] very good," Littler said. "I actually saw it yesterday or the day before. I didn't want to see it, but they've done a really good job.

"I'm really happy. Someone said you can see it from miles away. It's that big, it's that tall.

"At first, they wanted me to sit on the roof. I said no chance! I'll just stand on the pavement."

Littler's next match will come in Leicester on the Pro Tour on August 25 and 26 at Players Championship 27 and 28 as he looks to secure his place at the Players Championship Finals in Minehead.

articles.title: Commonwealth Games: England fight back to beat South Africa and reach netball semi-finals at Glasgow 2026
articles.summary: In a winner-takes-all group match to progress to the semi-finals, England came out on top against South Africa to secure a place in the last four; England overcame an early deficit to maintain their 100 per cent record of reaching the semi-finals at the Commonwealth Games
articles.body:
England fought back to beat South Africa 58-54 to reach the netball semi-finals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Both sides needed to win to book a spot in the last four and England roared back from an early 17-11 deficit after the first quarter to keep their hopes of a second Commonwealth gold alive.

The Vitality Roses will face New Zealand in the second of Saturday's semi-finals after Australia play Jamaica, then the gold and bronze-medal matches take place on Sunday.

  • Sky Sports on WhatsApp: Breaking news, videos and analysis
  • Not got Sky? Get Sky Sports or stream contract-free on NOW
  • Choose the Sky Sports push notifications you want

"Shout out to Halimat Adio. She was unreal in that second quarter. So proud of her to bring us that energy and get us back in the game when we needed it," captain Francesca Williams told TNT Sports.

"We have been under pressure all week to perform so for us to finish out a game like that and ride the wave of goal for goal in the last quarter and come out on top, I'm so proud."

England got off to a nervy start as South Africa goal shooter Elmere van der Berg came flying out of the blocks with 16 goals from 19 attempts which silenced the crowd at the OVO Hydro.

Halimat Adio and Funmi Fadoju came on, which tightened up England's defence, and it changed the momentum of the match as they slowly got themselves back into the contest to trail just 29-28 at half-time.

England went on a charge early in the third quarter with five consecutive goals to move 35-30 ahead and took a 45-41 lead into the last quarter.

As the clock ran down, England calmly maintained their slender four-goal advantage as Olivia Tchine and Lois Pearson kept their composure up front to get Anna Stembridge's side over the line.

Stembridge stepped up to become head coach just four months before the Commonwealth Games after Jess Thirlby resigned.

Netball has been in the Commonwealth Games since 1998 but England have never won a medal when it has been held in the United Kingdom.

1pm: Australia vs Jamaica (semi-final 2)

Sunday August 2
9am: Bronze medal match
1pm: Gold medal match

articles.title: World Darts Championship: 2026/27 dates confirmed for Alexandra Palace with Sunday final in Great Hall for first time
articles.summary: The 2026/27 PDC World Darts Championship is set to break records with a Sunday final at Alexandra Palace's Great Hall and a new ballot procedure introduced with 180,000 tickets on offer
articles.body:
The Paddy Power PDC World Championship dates have been confirmed for Friday December 11 to Sunday January 3 with a record 180,000 tickets on offer.

In a major change for this year the tournament will be held in Alexandra Palace's Great Hall for the first time, which can accommodate over 5,200 spectators compared to the previous 3,200 limit.

Luke Littler went back-to-back in January when he defeated Gian van Veen in a one-sided final with the 19-year-old, who has already won the World Masters, UK Open, World Cup, World Matchplay and Premier League in 2026, ready to make it a hat-trick of wins.

  • Littler dominates Price to close out historic World Matchplay defence
  • Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results 📅
  • Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app 📱
  • Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺

For the first time in the event's history, tickets for the tournament will be allocated through a Wimbledon-style ballot, which will take place in two stages.

PDCTV annual members receive an exclusive priority window, giving them an increased opportunity to secure tickets ahead of the general ballot opening.

The PDC annual members ballot then opens at 12pm on Tuesday September 1 until Monday September 7.

The general ballot opens at 12pm on Tuesday September 8 and closes at 11.59pm on Monday September 14.

The first round will be starting four days earlier than in 2025 with 128 players involved - live on Sky Sports.

There will also be the usual Christmas break between December 24-27 with the tournament concluding after New Year's Eve.

Alexandra Palace has hosted the World Darts Championship since 2007.

articles.title: How Harsh fought through pain to script CWG history, now targets Asiad medal
articles.summary: Commonwealth Games News: NEW DELHI: Harsh Singh's right knee still swells. It still hurts. Every time the Indian judoka steps onto the mat, he is reminded of the ACL and menis.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Harsh Singh's right knee still swells. It still hurts. Every time the Indian judoka steps onto the mat, he is reminded of the ACL and meniscus tear that nearly derailed his career. But at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, pain took a back seat as the 23-year-old scripted history by becoming India's first-ever men's judo gold medallist."The pain never really goes away," Singh told TOI in an interview on Thursday. "Sometimes my knee still swells up and feels tight. During the CWG, I felt the pain and the knee occasionally got swollen. After surgery, the joint never became exactly the way it was before. There's always a little discomfort during fights. You have to ignore it and continue. The medal kept me going."The historic triumph came less than a year after Singh tore his ACL and meniscus while training at the Inspire Institute of Sport (IIS) in Aug 2025. Surgery followed in Oct last in Bengaluru before a year-long rehabilitation helped him return to competition."I was in rehabilitation for almost a year. The entire coaching team at the IIS, recovery specialists and Spencer sir (Mackay, S&C expert) helped me throughout. They rebuilt my strength step by step. Because of the IIS and their entire team, I was able to come back on the mat, qualify for the CWG and represent India," he said.The comeback demanded another battle off the mat. Months away from competition saw his weight rise to nearly 72kg, forcing him to shed more than 12kg to return to his 60kg category. Gold at a ranking tournament and bronze at the senior National championships sealed his place in India's CWG squad.Despite lingering discomfort, Singh dominated in Glasgow, with only a hard-fought semifinal stretching him before he clinched the historic title."The semifinal (against the Australian Pedro Carlos) was the toughest. In the 60kg category, even a small point can decide the match. We didn't want to concede anything and stayed aggressive," he recalled.With CWG gold secured, Singh has already shifted his attention to next year's Asian Games. Training stints in Japan and South Korea are part of his preparations as he looks to bridge the gap with Asia's best."I want to improve my speed, grip and strength. Japanese and Korean players are very fast, so training there will help," he said.Born into a modest family, with his father working as a daily-wage labourer, Singh once trained without owning a judo uniform. Support from the govt's schemes and a privately funded athletes' training centre changed the course of his career."My life has changed because of this medal. More people have started noticing judo," he said. "But the best compliment came from my family. They told me, 'You have made the entire family proud.' That meant more than anything else."Having conquered injury to create CWG history, Singh's next aim is clear â turning a gritty comeback into an Asian Games podium finish.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Days after historic CWG gold, Dilip Gavit leaves without meeting Raj Thackeray after two-hour wait
articles.summary: Commonwealth Games News: Just days after scripting history for Indian para athletics at the Commonwealth Games, gold medallist Dilip Gavit found himself making headlines for a.
articles.body: Just days after scripting history for Indian para athletics at the Commonwealth Games, gold medallist Dilip Gavit found himself making headlines for a very different reason. The 23-year-old sprinter, who became India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the men's 100m T47 event, waited for nearly two hours to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray in Nashik on Thursday before leaving without the meeting taking place.Invited, but left waitingAccording to Gavit's coach quoted by PTI, Vaijanath Kale, the para-athlete had been invited to meet Thackeray during the MNS chief's visit to Nashik. However, despite arriving at the scheduled venue, Gavit and his coach were made to wait for nearly two hours. A video from the venue showed MNS workers requesting the duo to wait longer while trying to explain that Thackeray was occupied."We were waiting for quite some time... Sir is busy. We will meet him later," Kale is heard saying in the video before they eventually left.A champion who made history in GlasgowThe incident came just days after Gavit delivered one of India's biggest moments at the Commonwealth Games. Clocking a Games-record 10.71 seconds, the Nashik sprinter won the men's 100m T47 gold medal, leading a historic Indian one-two finish alongside Mohammed Basil Morssinganakath, who claimed silver. The victory marked India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medal in para athletics 100m T47.A journey built on resilienceGavit's success carries a deeper significance given his remarkable journey. Born into an economically disadvantaged tribal family in Maharashtra, he lost his right arm in a childhood accident. His life changed when coach Vaijanath Kale took him under his wing at the age of 12, supporting his education and athletic development. After winning gold in Glasgow, Gavit emotionally dedicated the medal to Kale, crediting his coach for transforming his life.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

Clocking a Games-record 10.71 seconds, the Nashik sprinter won the men's 100m T47 gold medal, leading a historic Indian one-two finish alongside Mohammed Basil Morssinganakath, who claimed silver. The victory marked India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medal in para athletics 100m T47.A journey built on resilienceGavit's success carries a deeper significance given his remarkable journey. articles.title: Raymond van Barneveld fined and suspended over inappropriate behaviour and offensive language in latest Darts Regulation Authority case list
articles.summary: Dutch darts legend Raymond van Barneveld, Cameron Menzies and Dom Taylor are among the high-profile players named in the latest Darts Regulation Authority (DRA) case list, published for the first time since 2022
articles.body:
Five-time world champion Raymond van Barneveld has been fined and suspended by the Darts Regulation Authority for inappropriate behaviour and offensive language.

The DRA, which is the independent body responsible for regulating the sport, particularly in events run under the umbrella of the PDC, WDF, Modus and ADC, has published an updated case list for the first time since 2022, listing all backdated hearings from January 2023 to June 2026, relating to various incidents that had occurred in both televised and non-televised competition.

Former world champions Rob Cross, Gary Anderson, Luke Humphries and Van Barneveld all feature in the case list, along with Cameron Menzies and Dom Taylor.

  • Littler dominates Price to close out historic World Matchplay defence
  • Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results 📅
  • Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app 📱
  • Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺

Van Barneveld, widely regarded as one of the sport's greatest-ever players, features in two separate incidents.

The first involves 'Inappropriate behaviour and using offensive language' at Players Championship 2 event in Wigan last year, resulting in a three-month suspension [suspended for 12 months] and £3,000 fine.

The second relates to 'failing to report damage caused to hotel room' following a Players Championship event in Germany, which resulted in a formal warning.

'Barney' is a five-time world champion having won the BDO tournament at Lakeside in 1998, 1999, 2003 and 2005 before making the move to the PDC the following year.

The doyen of Dutch darts made his mark by winning the 2007 PDC World Championship with a legendary final against Phil 'The Power' Taylor.

Sky Sports have contacted the DRA regarding Van Barneveld's fines.

Menzies handed four-month suspension

Menzies' sanction for his outburst at the World Championship in December has been revealed, with the Scot handed a four-month suspension, which ended last month, and receiving a £2,500 fine after he repeatedly punched the underside of the drinks' table on stage in frustration following his defeat to Charlie Manby.

The incident drew blood on his knuckles, which he then wiped on his face before walking off the stage.

Shortly after the incident, Menzies issued a statement apologising for his actions.

"First of all, I would like to apologise for what happened," said Menzies. "I am sorry that I reacted in the manner that I did.

"It's not an excuse, but I have had a lot of things on my mind recently and I suppose it all just became too much at the end.

"It has not been an easy time for me with my uncle Gary passing away recently. I saw him four days before he died and he gave a look which told he much he thought of me. He treated me like a son.

"Had I won the game against Charlie, my second match would have been on the day of Gary's funeral and that has not been lost on me in recent days.

"Let me say again, that's no excuse for what I did on the stage. It was the wrong thing to do and I don't want it to take anything away from Charlie. He played well and deserved his win.

"This is not how I would like people to view me. Yes I can get emotional at times, but not like that and that wasn't right."

Taylor's failed drugs test

Taylor's failed drugs test at the World Championship resulted in a six-month suspension until June 18, as well as a £1,275 fine in costs and the forfeiture of his £25,000 in prize money.

Taylor tested positive for cocaine and cannabis with the offence being his second which incurred a mandatory six-month ban under DRA rules.

"Accordingly, and taking into account all of the available evidence, the committee were satisfied that Mr Taylor's ingestion of both cocaine and cannabis occurred out of competition and was not following the commencement of the World Championship on 11th December 2025," the DRA statement read.

"Following on from this finding, the committee has determined that as this is Mr Taylor's second offence, then under these rules, he must serve a six month ban in line with 10.9 (a) and 10.9 (b) of UKAD Anti-Doping Rules 2021".

Taylor also lost his Tour Card as a result of the offence.

He had previously served a one-month ban in 2025 after failing a drugs test at the Players Championship Finals in November 2024. The ban was reduced from an initial two years after he agreed to undergo a UKAD-approved three-month substance abuse treatment programme.

Prakash Jiwa and Andy Jenkins both received hefty bans and were each made to pay costs of over £17,000 after being found guilty of match-fixing in the Modus Super Series from 2022-2023.
